title: Rounding and estimating
cover_sub: Round to tens, hundreds, decimal places and significant figures, then use rounding to estimate answers and check calculations.

parents.listen: Ask: which digit are you rounding to, and which digit decides? A child who can point to both digits has understood. When estimating, listen for rounding to one significant figure, not to the nearest whole number.

levels_long.d: Getting the basics: one step at a time.
levels_long.s: Year 8 standard: a few steps, some in context.
levels_long.e: A stretch: problems, reasoning and spotting mistakes.

briefing: Rounding makes a number simpler while keeping it close to the real value. Find the digit you're rounding to, then look at the next digit to the right: 5 or more, round up; 4 or less, leave it.
Decimal places (d.p.) are counted after the decimal point. Significant figures (s.f.) are counted from the first digit that isn't zero.
To estimate, round every number to 1 significant figure, then work out the easier calculation. Write ≈, which means approximately equal to.
method: Find the digit in the place you're rounding to, and draw a line just after it.
Look at the next digit along.
5 or more: add one to the digit before the line. 4 or less: leave it.
Whole numbers: fill in with zeros up to the decimal point. Decimals: stop at the line.

examples.question: Round 6.2753 to 2 decimal places.
steps: 5 or more, so the 7 goes up to 8.

examples.question: Round 0.04718 to 2 significant figures.
steps: The first digit that isn't zero is 4. Count 2 figures from there: 0.047 | 18.
The next digit is 1, so the 7 stays.
Don't remove the zeros at the front: they hold the place.

examples.question: Estimate the answer to 38.6 × 4.9.
steps: Round each number to 1 significant figure: 38.6 ≈ 40 and 4.9 ≈ 5.

e.blurb: Problems, reasoning and one piece of tampered evidence.

text: A whole number, rounded to the nearest ten, is 70.
What is the smallest it could be? What is the largest?
questions.working: 65 to 74 all round to 70; 75 rounds to 80.

text: Tickets cost £11.85 each. Estimate the cost of 38 tickets.
Is your estimate more or less than the real cost? Explain how you know.
questions.answer: 40 × £12 = £480. It's more than the real cost, because both numbers were rounded up. (The real cost is £450.30.)

text: Sam estimated 0.48 × 612. Find the mistake and give a better estimate.
questions.working: Rounding 0.48 to the nearest whole number makes it 0 and loses all the information.

questions.answer: 6 × 400.5 = 2400.5 = 480
questions.working: Dividing by 0.5 is the same as multiplying by 2.
questions.tip: How many halves are there in 240? Dividing by 0.5 doubles the number.

mistakes: Rounding the wrong digit, or counting significant figures from the decimal point instead of the first non-zero digit.
Dropping place-holder zeros: 45 672 to 2 s.f. is 46 000, not 46.
Writing 3.996 to 2 d.p. as 3.10 or 4. The answer is 4.00.
Rounding small decimals to 0 when estimating. Round to 1 significant figure instead: 0.48 ≈ 0.5.
closed_points: Round to decimal places and significant figures.
Estimate answers by rounding to 1 significant figure.
Explain whether an estimate is bigger or smaller than the real answer.
